title: Wanted LLMs to help me pick stocks. It destroyed my retirement hope
author: Electrical-Taro-4058
selftext:
This is a long long story. 

As a foreigner living in Singapore, it is such a weird place where everyday is summer. The whole island you can drive around in less than two hours, and somehow life still feel boring as hell.

Last Friday after work, I walked out of my office building like an NPC. At the gate I met a friend who does family office trading in the same building, so we went to a small bar, ordered a big beer and fries.

Then usual salaryman talks: boss is toxic, economy is bad, layoffs is coming, AI eating jobs again.

Then somehow we talked about early retirement.

We did some very rough math. Need around 1M USD in financial assets at least. If can make stable 10% annual return, maybe can semi-retire. Worst case go supermarket to be a cashier, at least no boss shouting at me. My current toxic work already giving me almost PTSD.

Then we talked about how much money you would make if you bought semiconductor stocks at the start of the year, and also the recent MRNA cancer vaccine phase 3 success news, which used AI-assisted design.

So I asked him, does your firm use AI for trading?

My friend looked very unimpressed

He said Trading is a lot about taste. LLMs are good at summarizing, but they don't have real trading taste.

I was not convinced.

Mainly because I saw that popular “daily LLM stock trading competition” thing before. It is kind of hype, but still interesting. But that experiment only gave models OHLCV. I feel this is a bit wrong. LLM's strength is not staring at few k lines. It should read news, earnings, filings, biz desc, earning callls, these kind of things.

Only giving OHLCV is not testing LLM. It is testing a bad quant model.

Also honestly, AI already killed so many jobs, helping me retire earlier should not be too much to ask.

So during the weekend I started. I wanted to test two questions:

1. If I give LLM the information visible at that time, can it beat the market?

2. If it looks like it can pick stocks, is it reading the information, or just using company stories it already knows?

**Round 1: the result was too good, so I doubted** 

I used early Jan 2023 as the decision date. I gave several LLMs point-in-time snapshots for a group of large cap stocks, and asked them to pick 10 stocks they wanted to hold for the next 90 days.

However the most tricky part is the point-in-time snapshot. The one that is really annoying to build.

I used yfinance, then tried polygon.io, then opened an FMP account, then did data cleaning until I hated my life, even with codex. Later I found news and historical context data is expensive as hell. Finally I used the snapshot API from plusefin.com.

OK, then I got something from plusefin.com. They are more like a formatted analyst packet. Company info, market data visible at that time, news, fundamentals summary. The useful thing is it can organize what was visible for a stock at a given date.

Then I charged 10 dollars into openrouter.com and tested several models. I did not test claude because too expensive.

Models roughly are:

gpt-5.5 deepseek-v4-flash-0731 glm-5.3-flash kimi-k2.7 and qwen3.8-max

The first round result was very exciting.

Several model portfolios strongly beat SPY. The best model was around +42.7% in 90 days, while SPY was around +7.5% in the same period.

Honestly when I saw this chart, I almost wanted to post directly:

\> I asked LLMs to pick stocks. They crushed SPY.

But I feel there must be something felt wrong.

Because these are all famous large cap stocks. After Jan 2023, everyone knows what happened with names like NVDA, META, TSLA. Current models very likely already saw this in training data. So maybe it is not doing research. Maybe it is just remembering the future.

This is very annoying.

Because if this is memory effect, then I can not get any alpha in fact .

So I kept digging.

**Round 2: random stock pool, still looks like something**

Next I changed to a randomly sampled sp 500 pool, 20 stocks. Same early Jan 2023 start, same 90-day holding period.

This time I did not use SPY as benchmark. Because if the random pool itself is more growth-ish, comparing with SPY is not so meaningful. So I used equal-weight portfolio of the same 20stock pool as benchmark.

Result was still pretty good.

The 20-stock equal-weight pool returned around +6.4%. The 10-stock portfolios selected by LLMs were around +10.6% to +12.7%.

At this point I was a bit excited, but also afraid to believe it.

If round 1 was only memory of big names like NVDA/META, then the random S&P 500 pool should be much weaker. But it still beat the same-pool benchmark.

But then another question came out:

 **Are ticker and company name itself the biggest cheat code?**

For example, when the model sees First Solar, Boeing, NXP Semiconductors, it is not just seeing a string. It sees a whole company narrative, industry position, historical news, and market feeling around that name.

Even more annoying, these names may also make the LLM remember their later performance.

So if I want to know whether it has some more pure trading taste, I need to remove the names.

Of course, this cannot fully remove model memory. But at least remove the most obvious clue: company identity.

 **Round 3: hide the stock names**

So I made a blinding version.

Same 20 stocks. Same early Jan 2023 decision date. Same 90-day holding period.

Difference is, all ticker and company names were replaced with anonymous IDs like Stock\_01, Stock\_02.

The model can still see the data and text structure inside the snapshot, but it cannot directly know if this is Boeing, First Solar, or Wells Fargo.

Then the result reversed.

In the visible ticker/company version, models had clear positive alpha on average.

In the blinded version, the strong alpha basically disappeared. Some models slightly beat, some underperformed. 

 It looked more like LLM can call a lot of semantic priors when it sees company identity.

Toxic result.

At least under anonymous condition, it did not show stable stock picking ability.

But this was actually the most interesting part of the experiment. It is not simply saying LLM is useless. It changed the question into:

Where does the LLM's investment judgement come from? From information visible at that time, from company identity and semantic context, or from market memory in training data?

When the model sees FSLR, it may think about solar, policy, growth stock, past performance, market narrative.

When it only sees Stock\_04, those things are gone.

Suddenly it feels less magic. Also less fun.

 **weekly rebalance was more embarrassing**

Finally I made a shorter-period version.

Still blinded snapshot, but changed to weekly rebalance. Every week I gave model the anonymous stock snapshots from that time, asked it to pick 10 stocks, and hold until next week.

Result was more direct

all models underperformed the same 20-stock weekly equal-weight benchmark.

Benchmark was around +9.1%. Models were around +4.5% to +5.6%.

From visible, to blinded, to blinded weekly rebalance, average alpha went down all the way.

Hard to cope.

 

**So the ending is I lost**.

My friend is probably right: LLM does not look like it can directly trade stocks, at least not in the way I imagined, like feed it some materials and it helps me retire early.

But I also don't think this experiment only says LLM is useless. At least it gave me a new thought:

\> If you don't control ticker/company identity, you may not know whether LLM is doing research, or just calling company narrative and historical memory.

In real world, investing is not pure numbers. Company name, industry position, management history, market narrative, these are all part of information. Human trader's taste also cannot be totally separated from these contexts.

At least should be able to do these:

1. Fix the date, try to make sure model only sees information visible at that time.

2. Separate ticker identity and test it alone.

3. Compare performance under visible and blinded conditions.

4. Save every snapshot, prompt, and portfolio the model saw.

I don't think the answer is LLMs are useless for finance. but we need better experiment design to know what exactly it is using to make decisions.

Next step I want to do a real forward-looking version. From now on, every week generate snapshot at fixed time, let model pick stocks, then record future performance in real time.

Then at least no more 2023 historical memory problem.

If people are interested, I can also organize the prompt, pool construction, and blinding method on github.

Finally, please give me a good reason why my experiment is actually wrong.

At least let me feel I still have hope to retire early.

comments.author: Slight_Ad_6375
comments.body: Don’t treat llm as a smart “human”. It’s not. Think of it as a very efficient way to turn ideas into code.

replies.author: Electrical-Taro-4058
replies.body: I agree. One of my trading system is using ai coding to do experiments and find out factors then turn it into code. But that's too traditional. I want to try if it can act like a financial expert

comments.author: hossein93
comments.body: I think you should go rule based method first then mount on LLM on rule based system smoothly!

replies.author: Electrical-Taro-4058
replies.body: how does the rule system look like. Any pseudo code?    BTW, the hardest part is to get an ideal history sandbox for LLM to back test.  Without backtesting I won't deploy any

replies.author: hossein93
replies.body:
Yeah — I mean something like this:

1. Build a deterministic baseline first:
   market state -> features -> fixed rules -> signal -> risk limits -> order

Pseudo:

if market_is_open:
    state = get_market_state()
    features = calculate_features(state)

    if risk_gate_passes() and entry_rules_pass(features):
        signal = create_signal(features)
        execute(signal, fixed_risk_rules)

Then add the LLM only as a bounded layer, for example:

context = structured_market_context(features, news, regime)
llm_output = LLM(context)

But the LLM is NOT allowed to place trades directly.
It can only:
- classify regime
- flag unusual conditions
- suggest confidence/risk scaling
- explain why a setup may be weak

Final execution still has to pass deterministic risk and execution rules.

For the history problem, I agree with you — that is probably the hardest part. I wouldn't let the model "remember" future information. I'd replay data sequentially with a strict timestamp cutoff, like a walk-forward sandbox, so at time T it can only see information that existed before T.

That way you can compare:
rule-based baseline
vs.
rule-based + LLM overlay

and see whether the LLM actually adds value instead of just sounding intelligent.

replies.author: Electrical-Taro-4058
replies.body: Great demo.   May I ask what kind of data you replayed to AI, the backtest part

replies.author: hossein93
replies.body:
I haven't run this exact LLM historical sandbox yet — I was describing how I would structure the experiment.

For the replay, I'd only expose information that was actually available at timestamp T, for example:

- OHLCV / market data up to T
- indicators or features calculated only from past bars
- current position / exposure / account state
- volatility and regime features
- if using news or sentiment, only items with an original timestamp <= T

Then I would build the LLM context at T, save its output, advance the simulation to T+1, and repeat.

So the LLM never sees the future candle, future P&L, revised data, or later news.

Something like:

historical stream
-> timestamp cutoff
-> structured context
-> LLM classification / recommendation
-> deterministic risk gate
-> simulated execution
-> advance one step

Then I'd compare exactly the same period using:

1. rule-based baseline
2. rule-based + LLM overlay

My main concern would be avoiding look-ahead leakage, because an LLM can appear very smart in a backtest if even a small amount of future context leaks into the prompt.

I haven't tested whether this would actually improve returns yet — that's the experiment I'd want to run.
